tagline.text: Seat of the Diocese of Kalookan, founded as a parish in 1815

location.label: Location
location.text: Corner of 10th Avenue and A. Mabini Street, Poblacion, Caloocan City

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Dry season, December–May (August 16 feast period excepted)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱50~300 (round-trip public transport within Metro Manila)

children.text: San Roque (St. Roch) Cathedral in Poblacion, Caloocan, was established as a parish in 1815 and became a cathedral when the Diocese of Kalookan was created in 2003. It carries traces of the 1899 Philippine–American War, and the National Historical Commission placed a marker here in 2022.

Caloocan Cathedral is a Roman Catholic church in the southern part of Caloocan City, north of Metro Manila proper, at the corner of 10th Avenue and A. Mabini Street in the Poblacion district. Its official name is the Cathedral Parish of San Roque, and the diocesan office lists its address at the same corner. On June 28, 2003, Pope John Paul II created the Diocese of Kalookan, and this church became its mother church, or cathedral. The diocese was carved out of the Archdiocese of Manila from southern Caloocan, Malabon and Navotas. The name can be confusing because maps and diocesan materials sometimes spell it Kalookan, so it helps to search with both spellings.

The church's history goes back to 1765. Fr. Manuel Vaquero, an assistant priest of the Tondo parish, is said to have started a small visita chapel together with local residents. The statues of San Roque and Nuestra Señora de la Soterraña de Nieva came to the community at that time. On April 8, 1815, Archbishop of Manila Juan Antonio de Zulaibar established it as a full parish, and construction of a larger church on the present site continued until it was reportedly completed in 1847. In 1889 the parish lost its status after failing to meet archdiocesan requirements, and it was revived in 1892.

For travelers, the most interesting part is its modern history. During the Philippine Revolution, the church is said to have been a gathering place for Katipunan members heading toward Balintawak. On February 10, 1899, General Antonio Luna took refuge here while fighting US forces, and the church was partly destroyed in the American attack. The US army later used the grounds as a field hospital, and in 1900 a regiment even used the church as a stable. The church was rebuilt in 1914, renovated in 1934, 1947, 1962 and 1979, and blessed by Cardinal Jaime Sin on November 30, 1981. In 2022 the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) and the diocese unveiled a historical marker for the church. It is known as the fourth parish in the country to receive such a marker.

The building is described as Baroque, but repeated renovations have changed its original look considerably. The ground level keeps statue niches and Tuscan pilasters, while the entrance portico and the flanking wings are described as later additions. The upper level has semicircular arched windows and a balustrade, with a two-tier bell tower rising in the center. It is not a glamorous tourist sight but an urban church where local parishioners come and go every day. That makes it a good stop in a slow historical walk alongside places such as Manila Cathedral and Intramuros. Black-and-white tiles were laid along the aisles in 1934, the facade was renovated in 1947, and side wings were added in 1962. In 2000 it was named a Jubilee Church, and after the altar and sanctuary renovation at the end of 2015, a dedication rite for the cathedral was held. In 2021 the church also opened a community pantry during the pandemic that helped many neighbors every day, so it feels not like a mere monument but like the center of a living local community.

blocks.title: A Baroque-style facade in the middle of the city

children.text: The ground level has statue niches and columns, and the upper level has semicircular arched windows and a balustrade. Through several renovations, the entrance portico and the side wings were added later. It is fun to tell the older parts from the newer additions.

A bell tower rises in two tiers at the center of the facade, topped by a cross. Because the surroundings are a busy urban area, it is hard to take in from afar, so look up at it from the street in front of the church.

It is said that early in the Philippine–American War, General Antonio Luna took shelter here from US forces and the church was partly destroyed. Records also say it later served as a field hospital and a stable, which shows that the church stood in the middle of the war.

blocks.title: On the road to Balintawak with the Katipunan

children.text: It is known as a place where Katipunan members gathered before heading to Balintawak. Looking at the church, you can recall the history of the area during the revolution.

Set up jointly by the National Historical Commission and the Diocese of Kalookan, this marker honors the role the parish played in the Philippine–American War. Check the marker's location and wording on site when you visit.

blocks.title: St. Roch and the bone relics

children.text: The church is dedicated to St. Roch, or San Roque, the patron saint of plague victims. In 2015, for the parish's 200th anniversary, a bone relic of San Roque sent by Pope Francis was placed on the altar, and a second relic arrived from Cebu in 2017.
It became a cathedral when the Diocese of Kalookan was created in 2003. The diocesan office stands at the same corner, so diocesan events and large Masses are often held here.

August 16 is the feast of San Roque every year. Worshippers crowd the church then and it is busier than usual, but you can see local devotion up close. The program changes each year, so check the church's announcements.

items.title: Half-day course
items.subtitle: Seeing the church and the Caloocan town center

children.text: Get off at LRT-1 Monumento or 5th Avenue station and take a jeepney or tricycle toward 10th Avenue in Poblacion. Travel time varies greatly with traffic, so allow plenty of time.
Look at the facade and bell tower from in front of the church and take photos. Avoid Mass times and quietly go in to see the main hall.
Look around the NHCP marker and the diocesan office area, and spend a little time praying or resting near the altar where the San Roque relic is kept.
Have lunch at a nearby eatery and walk around the Caloocan City Hall area, or return to Monumento and visit the Bonifacio Monument as well.
The church is a place where worshippers pray, so please be mindful of dress and noise. All times are examples only.

items.title: From Manila by LRT-1 and jeepney

children.text: From central Manila, a common way is to take LRT-1 and get off at 5th Avenue or Monumento station near the northern end of the line. Wikivoyage also lists these two stations.
Below the station, transfer to a jeepney or tricycle bound for Poblacion. Routes and fares can change, so ask drivers or locals on site and check the route in a transport app too.
From the airport a taxi or Grab is easier, but this stretch has heavy traffic and can take a long time.
Tell the jeepney driver to let you off at "San Roque Cathedral" or "Caloocan City Hall."
The church stands at the corner of 10th Avenue and A. Mabini Street, so search for this address in a map app. Some maps list the barangay differently, so go by the address.

The visit is mostly indoors, so the season matters little, but the walking parts are outdoors, so the dry season is more comfortable. During the day, late morning or early afternoon outside Mass times is quiet.

Around the August 16 feast of San Roque events are held and it gets crowded, and worshippers also fill the church during Holy Week and at Christmas in December. Mass times differ slightly by source, so it is safest to check the church's announcements.

The area around the church is not a tourist lodging district, so the usual plan is to stay in central Manila or Quezon City and visit as a round trip. Caloocan itself has places to stay, but check them yourself to fit your schedule. When coming from central Manila, plan to arrive around 10 a.m. so you avoid rush-hour crowding on LRT-1 and traffic on the roads.

For meals, expect Filipino home cooking at local restaurants in the streets around the church or at simple eateries near the market. Rather than recommending a particular famous restaurant, it suits the place to simply enjoy the local atmosphere. Having a good breakfast before you go lets you choose a lunch spot at leisure after your visit.
The church is called San Roque Cathedral and Caloocan Cathedral, so telling a jeepney driver "San Roque Cathedral" or "City Hall" will work.
Mass schedules differ between the diocesan site and various guide sites. Before you go, check the latest times on the church's Facebook page.
During Mass, refrain from taking photos and making noise, and dress modestly with shoulders and knees covered.
Combining the visit with the Bonifacio Monument near Monumento lets you see Caloocan's history in one day.
The diocesan office is open on weekdays from 8 a.m. to noon and from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. If you have a visit inquiry, contact them during these hours.
The diocesan office number is (02) 8288-9116. It may change, so check before visiting.
If you need a guide or historical explanation, you can ask the diocesan cultural heritage office in advance. A reply is not guaranteed.
This is mainly a place of worship, so avoid entering or photographing for sightseeing during Mass, and watch your belongings in the crowded streets.
Caloocan's streets have heavy traffic and many jeepneys and tricycles, so be careful when crossing.
In crowded places, keep your phone and wallet in front of you and beware of pickpockets.
Mass times, feast events and transport fares change often, so check the latest announcements.
Some maps and guides list a different barangay number and postal code, so find the church by the address at the corner of 10th Avenue and A. Mabini Street.
Avoid traveling late at night and use app-based taxis such as Grab, which is safer.
